title: The on-call engineer is getting paged constantly for non-issues — what do you do?
summary: Tests whether you can diagnose alert-fatigue causes and fix the alerting design, not just tell the engineer to ignore the noise.

slides.markdown:
"Just tune it out" is the wrong answer, and the interviewer knows it — it treats alert fatigue as a personal-resilience problem instead of what it actually is: a design flaw in what's being alerted on.

The strong answer diagnoses the specific cause — wrong thresholds, or alerting on internal causes instead of user-facing symptoms — and fixes the alerting design itself, since an engineer who's learned to ignore pages will eventually ignore the one that actually matters.

Ask whether the alerts are false positives, or true-but-non-actionable — a real but minor blip is a different problem than an alert firing on something that isn't actually happening. Each needs a different fix: false positives need threshold or logic corrections; true-but-non-actionable alerts need to be rerouted, not eliminated.

Ask how many pages per shift this engineer is currently getting, and how many of those actually led to a real action. That ratio — pages taken versus pages that led to action — is the concrete number that tells you how bad the problem actually is, rather than relying on "it feels like a lot."

Alert on user-facing symptoms, not internal causes, and raise thresholds where noise correlates with no real impact. This reframes the diagnosis question from "is this alert wrong" to "is this alert measuring the right thing at all" — many noisy alerts aren't technically incorrect, they're just measuring something that was never the right signal to page on.

The fix usually isn't "alert on less" — it's "alert on what's actually actionable and tied to user impact," which sometimes means removing an alert and sometimes means adding a better one in its place.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: replacing a cause-based alert with a symptom-based one
slides.markdown:
| | Per-server CPU alert | SLO burn-rate alert |
|---|---|---|
| Fires on | Any CPU spike, including routine batch jobs | Actual consumption of user-facing error budget |
| Actionability | Low — often nothing is actually wrong | High — directly tied to something worth waking up for |
| Noise | Frequent false alarms | Only fires when it matters |

The CPU alert is noisy because CPU usage alone doesn't tell you whether users are affected — a batch job spiking CPU at 3am might be completely routine. An SLO burn-rate alert only fires when real user-facing reliability is actually at risk, which is a fundamentally more useful trigger for waking someone up.

An on-call engineer is paged 8 times overnight for "disk usage above 80%" on a service where that's completely normal steady-state behavior thanks to routine log rotation timing — none of the 8 pages required any action.

The correct fix is removing that alert entirely, or moving it to a non-paging dashboard — not tuning the threshold up by 5%, which would just delay the same non-actionable noise rather than eliminate it. The threshold was never the problem; alerting on this metric at all, for this service, was the problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: symptom-based versus cause-based alerts
slides.markdown:
![Checkout error rate as a symptom that pages immediately versus a pod restart as a cause that usually self-heals](assets/symptom-vs-cause-alert.svg)

"Checkout error rate above 1%" is a **symptom** — direct evidence users are affected — and should page immediately. "One of 50 pods restarted" is a **cause** — usually self-healing infrastructure noise — and shouldn't page on its own unless it recurs repeatedly or correlates with an actual symptom.

The distinction is what separates a page worth waking someone up for from one that's really just internal telemetry masquerading as an incident.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Cutting noisy alerts risks cutting a rare-but-real signal along with the noise.

| Risk of cutting too little | Risk of cutting too much |
|---|---|
| Alert fatigue persists, real pages get missed in the noise | A rare but genuine failure mode goes undetected because its alert was removed |

The fix isn't "alert on less" as a blanket rule — it's "alert on what's actually actionable and tied to user impact," which sometimes means adding a better alert rather than just removing a bad one. Treating this purely as a volume-reduction exercise risks cutting the wrong things.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: you've cut alert volume in half — how do you know you didn't cut real signal?
slides.markdown:
Review incidents retroactively for the following month, and check whether any of them would have been caught earlier by an alert that was removed in the cut. That's the actual measure of whether the cut was safe — not a feeling that things seem quieter, but a concrete check against what actually happened afterward.

This review should be treated as mandatory, not optional, precisely because the risk of cutting real signal is real and the only way to catch a mistake here is by comparing against subsequent incidents, not by re-examining the alert definitions in isolation.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: some paged alerts really were true, just not actionable
slides.markdown:
Route true-but-non-actionable alerts to a non-paging channel — a dashboard, a daily digest — rather than a 2am page, reserving actual paging for what genuinely needs immediate human action.

This distinguishes "delete" from "deprioritize": a true signal that doesn't need immediate action still has value (it might matter in aggregate, or over time), it just doesn't belong in the same channel as something that needs someone woken up right now. Conflating the two channels is often exactly what causes alert fatigue in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: silencing or deprioritizing alerts wholesale
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The engineer is overwhelmed — let's just mute or deprioritize a bunch of alerts to give them relief."

**Why it's wrong:** silencing alerts wholesale, without fixing what they alert on and why, doesn't address the underlying design flaw — it just changes which failures go unnoticed. If a muted alert happened to be the one true signal in the noise, you've traded alert fatigue for a real outage nobody caught.

**Correct model:** fix the alerting design itself — alert on symptoms, route true-but-non-actionable signals elsewhere, remove genuinely useless alerts — rather than blanket-suppressing pages as a stopgap for engineer burnout.

Diagnose first: are the alerts false positives, or true-but-non-actionable? Then alert on user-facing symptoms (checkout error rate) rather than internal causes (one pod restarting), and route true-but-non-actionable signals to a non-paging dashboard instead of a 2am page.

The fix isn't blanket volume reduction — it's alerting on what's actually actionable and tied to user impact, which sometimes means adding a better alert, not just removing a noisy one. After any cut, verify against real incidents in the following month that you didn't remove genuine signal along with the noise.
